claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has a primarily FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy has a relatively homogeneous microstructure with minimal pre-existing porosity or oxide formation.
Selective oxidation of Al and Ti governs elevated-temperature degradation of this alloy.
Oxidizing exposure produces brittle, non-adherent mixed oxide bands along grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary oxide bands locally deplete matrix constituents.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxides and metallic matrix generates high stresses.
Oxide formation, local depletion, and mismatch stresses accelerate intergranular cracking and catastrophic failure.
Under reducing conditions, incomplete oxide formation causes internal void growth through diffusion-driven processes.
Reducing exposure can cause localized embrittlement and ultimately promote intergranular cracking under stress.
Oxidizing exposure at 900°C for 100 hours should produce thicker and more continuous oxide layers than the as-manufactured baseline and reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure should measurably deplete Al and Ti at grain boundaries.
Oxidizing exposure should increase intergranular crack density and reduce mechanical integrity relative to the starting state.
Reducing exposure should produce thinner, patchier oxide formation and internal voiding.
Catastrophic failure should be more pronounced in the oxidizing regime than in the reducing regime.
The proposed degradation behavior applies approximately from 800°C to 1000°C for exposures around 100 hours under the specified gas compositions.
Outside the stated temperature or time range, additional or alternative degradation mechanisms may become active.
Additive-manufacturing-induced local microsegregation may influence degradation behavior.
